a. $f$ increases where the drawn graph is positive: $x<0$ or $x>4$. It decreases where the graph is negative: $0<x<4$.

b. At $x=0$, $f'$ changes from positive to negative, so $f$ has a local maximum. At $x=4$, $f'$ changes from negative to positive, so $f$ has a local minimum.

c. $f''$ is the gradient of the drawn graph. At $x=0$ this gradient is zero but remains negative on both sides, so the concavity of $f$ does not change.

At $x=3$ the drawn graph changes from falling to rising. Thus $f''$ changes from negative to positive, and $f$ has an inflection at $x=3$ only.

a. The graph is below the axis for $x<-1$ and for $-1<x<2$, so $f$ is concave down on both intervals. It is above the axis for $x>2$, so $f$ is concave up there.

b. At $x=-1$, $f''$ is zero but does not change sign, so there is no inflection. At $x=2$, $f''$ changes from negative to positive, so $f$ has an inflection there.

c. No. A horizontal inflection also requires $f'(2)=0$, which this graph does not establish.

examples.derivation: The plotted cubic is x^3-12x+1, with derivatives 3x^2-12 and 6x. Stationary points occur at -2 and 2, and concavity changes at 0. The qualitative derivative plots have the correct zeros and signs. Independently, f'(-3)=15>0, f''(-3)=-18<0, f''(-2)=-12<0, f(0)=1>0 and f'(2)=0.

The plotted quartic is 3x^4/4-4x^3. Its derivatives are 3x^2(x-4) and 3x(3x-8). The first derivative remains negative across 0 and changes from negative to positive at 4. The second derivative has signs positive, negative, positive across 0 and 8/3. Both qualitative derivative plots are consistent positive rescalings.

The drawn first derivative is x^3(x-4)/8, positive outside (0,4) and negative inside. Thus f has a maximum at 0 and minimum at 4. Its derivative, f'', is x^2(x-3)/2: negative on both sides of 0 and changing from negative to positive at 3. Only 3 is an inflection location.

The drawn second derivative is (x+1)^2(x-2)/2. It is negative on both sides of -1 and positive beyond 2. Consequently only 2 gives a change of concavity. The graph does not determine f'(2), so horizontalness cannot be concluded.

The solution sketch uses 3/x on [1,4]. Its derivatives are -3/x^2<0 and 6/x^3>0 throughout this interval. It decreases while its gradient becomes less negative, correctly illustrating decreasing at a decreasing rate.

Differentiating 2e^{-x} gives -2e^{-x}, then 2e^{-x}. These are respectively negative and positive everywhere, have no zeros, and approach 0 as x tends to infinity. The plotted functions and matching red/blue labels agree.

Differentiating 2sin x gives 2cos x, then -2sin x. On the restricted domain the second derivative vanishes at 0, pi and 2pi, and changes from negative to positive only at the interior zero pi. The solution plot correctly reflects the question graph across the x-axis.
